**Summary:**
Sparse rewards in goal-conditioned RL is a challenging problem. This paper addresses this problem by decomposing the original task of reaching the goal, to smaller tasks of reaching subgoals instead. To achieve that, they train (1) a recursive subgoal predictor that builds on top of the Sub-Goal Tree (SGT) formulation, and (2) a goal-conditioned Soft Actor Critic (SAC) agent that gets rewards when subgoals are met. These models are trained in tandem, and the main novelty of this paper is that each model makes the learning of the other model easier. They show in experiments that this method works well in navigation tasks, as well a control task of walker 2D.

**Summary:**
The paper proposes a hierarchical algorithm for goal generation in goal-conditioned RL. Specifically, SGT from Jurgenson’20 is used to hierarchically produce a tree of subgoals with a subgoal policy, and a downstream goal-conditioned RL agent is trained on these subgoals instead of just the final goal. The subgoal policy is trained with a mix of a dense and a learned reward, while the downstream policy is trained with sparse reward.

**Summary:**
The paper proposes new nonlinear bandit and reinforcement learning algorithms whose sample complexity toward local maxima are bounded by the sequential Rademacher complexity of particular loss functions (and do not depend on the action dimension). An interesting insight obtained in this paper is that when dealing with nonlinear models and dynamics (in settings where the action dimension may be very large), maximizing the virtual return suggested by a strong online learner (with carefully augmented loss) may lead to good convergence guarantees to local maxima.

**Summary:**
This paper studies model-based nonlinear bandit and reinforcement learning and proposes the ViOlin algorithm (Virtual Ascent with Online Model Learner). The main contributions are as follows.

1) For bandit problems, with deterministic reward functions satisfying Assumption 2.1 (Lipschitz over continuous actions, smooth over actions, and the third order derivative over action is bounded), and with sublinear sequential Rademacher complexity, they show that the ViOlin algorithm achieves an $\epsilon$ approximate local maximum using $\tilde{O}(\epsilon^{-8})$ iterations, which does not depend on the dimension of action space.

Some instantiations are shown, including linear bandit with finite model class, with sparse or structured model vectors, and two-layer neural nets, which is the first result of non-linear bandit with neural network parameterization.

The main idea is to fit the estimation of gradient and Hessian, and show that the current greedy action can be improved until the parameter is close enough to an approximate local maximum.

2) For RL, with deterministic transition, and Assumptions 4.1 and 4.2 (regularity of value function and policy), they show that the similar ViOlin (Algorithm 2) achieves an $\epsilon$ approximate local maximum using also sublinear iterations.

The difference with bandit design is that the loss function is using one-step model prediction errors rather than gradient and Hessian.

3) The authors show some lower bound results. In particular, (i) using ReLU activations in one-layer neural network bandits, finding global optimal action takes exponentially large iterations. (ii) the failure of Eluder dimension: one-layer neural networks has its Eluder dimensions exponentially large. (iii) the failure of UCB: with linear reward function, and two-layer neural network as the hypothesis function class, UCB would take exponential sample complexity to find the optimal action.

**Summary:**
This paper considers learning in deterministic bandit and reinforcement learning problems with function approximation. They quantify the complexity of the function class using the sequential Rademacher complexity of a related loss function (although in some settings, it is not super clear how this relates to the complexity of the reward/value function). In the bandit setting, they provide a general regret bound and instantiate this for various different assumptions on the model, including two layer neural networks, which is a nice result. To extend their results to reinforcement learning some assumptions are made so that the value function can be written as a non-linear function of the policy parameters and optimized accordingly. They then provide a slightly simpler loss function and show that the sample complexity can be bounded in terms of the sequential Rademacher complexity of this. Finally, the authors provide some interesting lower bounds showing that finding a global maximum is exponentially hard, and motivating them to study the sample complexity to find an approximate local maximum.

**Summary:**
This work investigates model-based bandit and RL under non-linear function approximations. In particular, it focuses on convergence to approximate local maxima under deterministic reward (and deterministic dynamics for RL). Several technical results are derived showing that the presented model-based algorithm can have a favorable sample complexity that only depends on the sequential Rademacher complexity of the model class. The paper also contains some hardness results to better contextualize the contribution of this work.

This submission provides a rigorous theoretical analysis; the proofs appear correct and the assumptions are clearly stated. My main concern is reproducibility: no code is provided and several hyperparameters are unreported. The related-work coverage is adequate. Overall the significance for the broader community seems modest.

**Summary:**
This paper concerns referring expression comprehension (REC) and segmentation (RES). It proposes a unified one-step approach for both tasks through multi-task training. The proposed architecture is based on DETR, with a twist on context encoder to encode query caption and query encoder to encode each referring expression / entity. Comprehensive experiments are conducted over mainstream REC and RES datasets. Significant empirical improvements are observed.

**Summary:**
The paper proposes two modifications to DETR: 1) adding language input; 2) directly predict boxes from language phrase queries, instead of using random object queries and a set loss.

The result is a visual grounding model without limitation of the pre-trained object detection that is prevalent in previous vision-and-language models (e.g., ViLBERT/VL-BERT/UNITER…). It sets state-of-the-art results on grounding benchmarks such as Flirckr30K and RefCOCO. The model also opens door to building vision-and-language models without the limit of the pre-trained object detector.

Despite some limitations of the current model design, the paper stands in between traditional object detection and transitional vision-and-language modeling and shows promise and could lead to a good discussion.

**Summary:**
In this paper, the authors propose a one-stage multi-task framework for referring expression comprehension (REC) and segmentation (RES). They learn a single transformer based architecture with two separate heads for the bounding box regression and segmentation. It enables contextualized reasoning by taking as input the entire image, all referring query phrases of interest and the complete lingual context. They outperform state-of-the-art on various datasets for both these tasks and validate their design choices by ablation studies.

**Summary:**
In this paper, the authors modify the DETR object detector to approach the referring expression comprehension and segmentation tasks (REC and RES). The language referring is taken as the decoder query to generate the box/mask prediction. The proposed method outperforms the SOTA on multiple standard REC and RES benchmarks.

**Summary:**
This paper shows experimentally that training on generated data (from a generative model not trained on external data) can improve adversarial robustness.  Surprisingly, even a class-conditional Gaussian generative model can improve adversarial robustness. The paper additionally provides sufficient conditions for generated data to help adversarial robustness.

**Summary:**
This work shows that data augmentation using good generative models helps improve adversarial robustness. Various experiments are conducted to show the importance of the quality of the generated images. The proposed method achieves state-of-the-art adversarial accuracy on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 datasets, while the clean accuracy is not sacrificed.

**Summary:**
This paper examines whether using additional generated data can improve the robustness through adversarial training.  They propose several conditions for generated data to best improve the performance of adversarial training and validate the impact of these conditions empirically.  They evaluate the performance of several generative models (DDPM, VDVAE, BigGAN, Class conditional gaussian) on improving robust performance and demonstrate that using samples from DDPM, they are able to outperform many models using external data in training.

The paper tackles an interesting problem. However, the novelty is limited: the proposed method is a straightforward combination of two existing techniques. The writing is also difficult to follow in Sections 3-4, with undefined notation. On the positive side, the experimental evaluation is thorough, covering five datasets with proper ablations.

**Summary:**
The paper proposes to improve robustness of neural networks against adversarial attacks without using any additional data. For it, they make use of samples generated by a generative model as their proxy for additional data. They want the additional samples to be diverse enough, and list additional conditions needed for robustness to improve using generated data. Empiricall they obtain strong results, often performing better than the methods that use additional data.

**Summary:**

The submission presents convergence results for clipped stochastic gradient methods without the sub-Gaussian assumption.

The subject of the submission is of interest to the NeurIPS community. As we find that some of our most difficult problems exhibit heavy-tailed noise, how to handle it in stochastic optimization is becoming more and more relevant.


My understanding of the main contributions of the paper over existing work is that this submission considers $\nu$-Hölder continuity (interpolating between Lipschitz functions and function with Lipschitz gradients) without assuming the stochastic gradients be sub-Gaussian (but still having bounded variance)
- For the case $\nu = 0$ (Lipschitz functions), recovers tighter bounds (logarithmic dependence on the confidence level $\beta$ instead of polynomial) than naïve applications of Markov's inequality to results in expectation. 
- For the case of $\nu = 1$ (Lipschitz gradient), the claimed contribution over the existing results of Gorbunov et al. [14] is that the problem need only be smooth in a ball around a minimum.

**Summary:**
This paper aims to obtain the high probability convergence for the convex stochastic optimization problem when the stochastic gradient of the objective function is not assumed to be sub-Gaussian. While this goal has been achieved in two recently proposed optimizers by exploiting the gradient clippings technique under the smoothness assumption on the objective, this paper considers the more general setting when corresponding gradient only satisfies a Holder continuity condition. This condition recovers the smooth and non-smooth settings when an extra parameter takes extreme values. In such a more general problem formulation, the authors propose new step-size schemes such that the convergence rate of the aforementioned optimizers (designed for smooth problems) can be smoothly extrapolated to the non-smooth setting.

**Summary:**
The authors proposed  clipped-SSTM and its restart version for stochastic nonsmooth optimization with heavy tailed noise. A detailed convergence analysis shows the theoretical advantage of the proposed algorithm. Experiments on real models (Bert) show that clipped-SSTM outperforms standard SGD methods.

**Summary:**
This paper analyzes the clipped SGD and clipped SSTM algorithm on generalized smooth objectives with Hölder-continuous gradients. They consider the case where the assumption of sub-Gaussian noise is not needed. They modified the stepsize in the clipped SSTM algorithm to fit the Hölder-continuity assumption. Theoretical analysis is conducted with convergence rates presented.

**Summary:**
The paper tackles the important problem of high-probability convergence bounds for machine learning optimisation problems. Traditional analyses are done in expectation, which have been shown to not accurately represent all possible training outcomes; hence the need for tighter studies.
In this paper, in the specific setting of convex, non-smooth losses with heavy tailed noise, a new high-probability bound is introduced for two algorithms. What sets it apart from previous bounds is that there is no direct negative dependency on the confidence bound (only logarithmic ones); and that in some cases it matches the non-heavy tailed noise bound.
Numerical experiments illustrating the theoretical results are presented.

**Summary:**
This paper shows that any distribution can be decomposed into a number of disjoint distributions, each admitting a Forster transform, which has anti-concentration properties. An application of this decomposition is to learning halfspaces in the Massart noice model.

**Summary:**
This paper presents an algorithm to compute a certain decomposition of a point set known as a Forster decomposition. Roughly speaking this guarantees 
1. mean 0 and  close identity covariance
2. all points with norm close to one.
Each of these conditions is easy to achieve (via PCA and rescaling respectively),  the challenge is getting them to hold simultaneously.
The kind of mapping they seeks is an invertiable linear transformation followed by rescaling. 

While such a mapping may not always exist, it was known that the only "obstructions" are dense subspaces (in the extreme think of the same point repeated many times). The main algorithm in this paper allows one to find these obstructions efficiently. One can then iteratively  remove these points and keep going. This gives a decomposition into O(d) many subspaces and a good mapping for the points within each subspace.

The main application of this result is a learning algorithm for halfspaces in the Massart noise model whose sample complexity is independent of the bit-length of the inputs. The running time still depends polynomially on the bit lengths (inevitable by a reduction from LP). They key idea is that the mapping they use preserves the existance of a good homogenous halfspace classifier.

**Summary:**
This paper studies the problem of learning halfspaces under Massart noise in the absence of distributional assumptions on the x's. Previous works have given algorithms for this problem which achieve error eta + eps in time and sample complexity polynomial in d, 1/eps, and the bit complexity b of the x's. Removing the dependence on bit complexity in the runtime for the closely related problem of linear programming is a major open question, but more modestly one could hope to remove this dependence in the sample complexity, and this is the main result of this paper, which it achieves using a modification of the improper learner from [DGT19].

The main bottleneck that leads to the b dependence in previous algorithms is a preprocessing step due to Dunagan-Vempala that essentially reduces to the large margin case by removing some outliers so that no point among the remaining points S is far from S in Mahalanobis. The present work circumvents this as follows. For the preprocessing step, instead of outlier removal, one could also just try placing the dataset in approximate radial isotropic position. This is a technique that has been useful in a variety of other applications like subspace recovery, the Paulsen problem, communication complexity, etc. 

Unfortunately, not every dataset can be placed in radial isotropic position, for instance if some m-dimensional subspace is "heavy" in the sense that it contains more than an m/d fraction of the points. As shown in [HKLM20], this is the only obstruction, and the main contribution of the present work is to make this fact algorithmic, i.e. to give an algorithm for finding a heavy subspace such that the part of the dataset in that subspace can be placed in radial isotropic position.

Then to get the application to learning under Massart noise, whenever one needs to run the outlier removal step, just use the above algorithmic result to identify a heavy subspace, place those points in radial isotropic position, and run one step of the algorithm for learning large-margin halfspaces under Massart noise on those points to make progress.

**Summary:**
This paper studies the problem of finding a Forster transformation of a given distribution. The goal of a Foster transform is to transform an arbitrary distribution into a distribution that has good anti-concentration properties: in particular, one would like the transformed distribution to have its second moment matrix equal to a scaled identity matrix and the points from the distribution should also have Euclidean norm 1. For this problem, they give an algorithm that runs in weakly polynomial time. The algorithm itself uses the ellipsoid algorithm to solve SDPs and LPs.

As an application of their algorithm for finding Forster transforms, they consider the problem of PAC learning halfspaces under Massart noise. They show that there is an algorithm whose sample complexity is strongly polynomial and running time is weakly polynomial. Previously, the work of Diakonikolas et al. showed that there is an algorithm whose sample complexity and running are both weakly polynomial whereas, information-theoretically, it is known that the sample complexity can be strongly polynomial. So the present paper closes this gap up to polynomial factors.

**Summary:**
The paper considers the problem of recovering a mixture of unknown sparse vectors from noisy and noiseless sign responses. A response is the sign of the inner product between a randomly sampled unknown sparse vector from the mixture and a query vector (designed or random), up to some noise. The main contribution of the paper is to show existence of an algorithm that can recovery the support of the unknown vectors in the presence of noise. In the noiseless case and under mild assumptions on the uniqueness of the support set of the unknown sparse vectors and a bound on the size of the non-zero entries in these unknown vectors, the authors show existence of an algorithm that can estimate the sparse vector up to an arbitrary precision. The precision of the estimation depends inversely on the number of queries.

**Summary:**
This paper considers learning a family of \ell unknown k-sparse n-dimensional vectors from mixture of 1-bit repsonses.  In particular, the authors propose a novel robust support recovery algorithm that works without any additional assumption. For robust support recovery, they try to reduce the problem to a problem of quantitative group testing, and they make use of a notion that generalizes cover-free families, which are previously used in the context of various 1-bit compressed sensing problems in [1,12,13]. Based on the reconstructed support of all unknown vectors in the family, the authors provide noiseless approximate vector recovery guarantees under the assumptions that the support of any unknown vector is not fully contained in the support of any other unknown vector from the family and the magnitude of each entry can be bounded from below and above.

**Summary:**
The paper studies the problem of learning a family of $l$ unknown $k$-sparse vectors. For any query point, we are given the sign of the inner product between a vector from the family (chosen uniformly at random) and the query point. In this setting they consider two problems. In the first problem, they propose a procedure along with guarantees (see Theorem 1) for estimating the supports of each vector in the family where the query responses can be noisy (the signs can be flipped). For the second problem, they consider estimating each vector in the family albeit in a noiseless setting. For this problem, they propose a two-stage algorithm for approximately recovering the vectors in the family, with performance guarantees (in Theorem 2). The performance guarantee for a single-stage algorithm has also been provided in Theorem 3.

**Summary:**
 The paper addresses a generalized problem in 1-bit compressed sensing, e.g. considered in the NeurIPS 2020 paper [12]. The problem is to estimate ALL of l unknown k-sparse vectors from 1-bit noisy measurements based on q query vectors (See (1)) in terms of support recovery (Problem 2) and approximate recovery (Problem 1). 

 The goal of this paper is information-theoretic derivation of sufficient conditions on q, for which there are some algorithm and query vectors such that the support of all sparse vectors can be recovered with high probability (Theorem 1) or such that all sparse vectors can be recovered with negligibly small precision (Theorems 2 and 3). Theorem 1 is proven under some mild assumptions while [12] postulated an assumption (See [Assumption 1, 12]). On the other hand, Theorems 2 and 3 are proven under Assumption 1 in the submitted paper, which is weaker than [Assumption 1, 12].

**Summary:**
This paper studies the problem of learning multiple sparse signals from a mixture of 1-bit measurements, also referred to as mixture of linear classifiers. It proposes algorithms for both support recovery (with corrupted measurements) and value recovery (with noiseless measurements), which come with theoretical guarantees.

**Summary:**
This paper proposed an interesting learning approach to extend the visual question generation task. The authors continue to address the one image to many questions limitations and follow the setting of double visual and answer hints. Unlike the previous method, which leverages the rule-based method to obtain rough visual regions and learns to generate questions under the guidance of double hints faithfully, they cast the problem as a weakly supervised problem and optimize it with noisy supervision. More precisely, they regard the visual hints as a hidden constraint instead of a certain result. The proposed method outperforms existing methods on both VQA and COCO-QA tasks.

**Summary:**
This paper focuses on the visual question generation (VQG) problem. Given an image and an answer, the goal is to generate a relevant and understandable question that can be answered by the given answer. A recent paper proposes to leverage visual hints, i.e., regions of interest in the given image, to improve the performance of VQG. The visual hints could be generated based on similarity matching. However, such automatically generated visual hints are noisy. To fully take advantage of the noisy visual hints, this paper proposes a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) based framework DH-GAN to enable weakly supervision of ground truth questions. It would first identify suitable visual hints, and then generate the question based on the visual hints and the answer. Intensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of DH-GAN.
